title: Calling other services: REST, RPC and gRPC
goal: By the end, you can explain why a call to another program can end with no answer at all, write down what such a call sends in two styles (REST and gRPC), give every call a deadline, spread calls over several copies of a program, and retry a payment without charging the card twice.
opening:
Picture buying a book online. You press Pay, and the page spins. After a few seconds it says: Something went wrong. Please try again. Under the button, in small print: please don't press Pay twice.

Did you pay? The page doesn't know either. The shop's program asked another program, far away, to charge your card, and no answer came back in time. Maybe the question got lost. Maybe the card was charged and the answer got lost.

Pressing Pay again feels safe, and the shop's programmers feel the same pull: if a call fails, make it again. That's how we treat a function call in our own code, and there it works.

In Data outlives code, two versions of one program shared a database. Now two programs talk over a network. In this lesson, we'll time a call to another program, write down what it sends in two styles, give it a deadline, spread calls over several copies, and build a retry that can't charge a card twice. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The bookshop's program asks the payment company's program to charge a card. It waits 2 seconds, gets no answer, and stops waiting. What does the bookshop's program know about the charge?
options: It failed: the payment program never got the request
It went through, but the answer was slow
Nothing: the charge may have failed, gone through, or still be in progress
It was cancelled, because the bookshop's program stopped waiting
warmup.why: Running out of time only tells you that no answer arrived. The request may have been lost on the way. The card may have been charged and the answer lost. Or the payment program may still be working on it. Nothing cancels a charge when the asking program stops waiting. The first option is the tempting one, because it's what a failed function call means inside one program: if it didn't return, it didn't happen. The first section shows why that rule stops holding across a network.

sections.h: A call to another computer can end in a way a local call can't
sections.body:
Let's start with a stopwatch. A function call inside your own program takes about a nanosecond, a billionth of a second. The Try below times one small function, `authorize`, which says yes or no to a payment, three ways on a laptop. Called directly, it takes about 1 ns. Called through gRPC inside the same program, about 10 µs (microseconds, millionths of a second). gRPC is a free toolkit, first built at Google, that lets one program call a function in another; the third section opens it up. Called through gRPC over the network to 127.0.0.1, the address a computer uses to reach itself, it takes about 75 µs. Between two machines in one data centre, a round trip (there and back) costs a few hundred microseconds. Between continents, it's about 70 ms.

Now meet the running example. An online bookshop has a program behind its Pay button, called checkout. To take the money, checkout asks the payment service to charge the card. A **service** is a program that keeps running on a computer, a server, and answers requests that other programs send it over the network. The program that asks is the client. In checkout's code, the request can look like any other call: `payments.charge("pay-1", 4000)`, with the amount in cents.

Making it look like that is an old dream. In 1984, Andrew Birrell and Bruce Nelson described the **remote procedure call** (RPC). A generated stand-in function, called a stub, packs the arguments into bytes, sends them, waits, and unpacks the answer, so a call to another machine looks like a local one. In 1994, Jim Waldo and three colleagues at Sun Microsystems, then a big computer maker, wrote "A Note on Distributed Computing" to say the dream was a mistake. They named four differences that no stub can hide. Latency, the time a call takes: four to five orders of magnitude longer (10,000 to 100,000 times), they wrote. Memory: a pointer into one program's memory means nothing in another. Concurrency: other clients call the same service at the same moment. And partial failure.

Partial failure is the one that costs money. A local call ends in one of three ways: it returns, it throws an exception, or the whole program dies, caller and all. A remote call has a fourth ending. Checkout sends `Charge(pay-1, 40.00 EUR)` and waits 300 ms. Nothing comes back. Maybe the request was lost, and nothing happened. Maybe the card was charged and the reply was lost. Maybe the payment service is still working. To checkout, all three look the same: a timeout, the moment it stops waiting. Waiting longer doesn't settle it.

Ordering from a shop by phone on a bad line feels the same. You give your order, and the line goes quiet. Your order is the request, their "got it" is the reply, and either one can vanish. Call back and order again, and you may get two parcels.

Keep this picture for the whole lesson: a request goes out, work happens, a reply comes back, and any of the three can go missing. The stepper walks through the endings. First, though, both programs must agree on what a request looks like. Next, we'll write that down.

try.title: Time a local call against a remote one
steps: Open `CallCostDemo.kt`. It times one small `authorize` function three ways: a direct call; gRPC inside one program, with all of gRPC's work but no network (the in-process transport); and gRPC over the network to 127.0.0.1.
Predict the ratio between the direct call and the call over 127.0.0.1. Is it 10, 1,000 or 100,000?
From the `labs` folder, run the command below. It takes about 5 seconds.

code.title: CallCostDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
local function call              about 1.1 ns per call
gRPC, in-process transport       median    10.96 us   p99    29.00 us
gRPC, HTTP/2 over 127.0.0.1      median    76.71 us   p99   197.92 us
```
Numbers vary with the computer and how busy it is (this run: an Apple laptop with JDK 25, the Java toolkit the labs use), but the ratios hold. About 1 ns against about 75 µs is a factor of about 70,000, close to Waldo's five orders of magnitude, with no real network in the way. The in-process line is the cost of gRPC itself: turning the request into bytes, the call machinery and a hand-off between threads. The median is the middle time, and p99 is the time that 99% of calls beat, so it shows the slowest 1%. A remote call's time also varies: here the slowest 1% took more than twice the median.

aside.title: Can't checkout ask whether the charge went through?
aside.body: Sometimes it can, if the payment service offers a lookup by payment number. But the lookup is a remote call too, with the same four endings. Worse, if the first request is still on its way or still running, the lookup truthfully says "no charge", and a moment later the charge happens. Check first, then charge, and a second charge can slip into the gap. The last section closes it another way: it makes the second attempt recognizable.

sections.h: REST: a few verbs on named things, and a contract you can check
sections.body:
Here's a payments API in the REST style. An API (application programming interface) is the set of requests a program accepts from other programs:

```text
POST /v1/charges                  create a charge
GET  /v1/charges/ch_77            read charge ch_77
POST /v1/charges/ch_77/refunds    refund it
```

Each line is an HTTP request. HTTP is the set of rules that web browsers and servers follow; the Networking track's lesson HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 over QUIC opens it up. A request starts with a method, a verb such as GET (read) or POST (create), and a path, the part of the web address after the server's name. Then come headers, lines of extra detail, and sometimes a body. The reply starts with a status code, a three-digit number such as `201 Created` or `404 Not Found`. Bodies are usually JSON, text made of names and values: `{"payment_id":"pay-1","amount_cents":4000}`.

REST comes from Roy Fielding's PhD thesis of 2000. It treats an API as a set of resources, things with names, each named by a URL, a full web address. Clients act on them with HTTP's few methods, and the rest comes from HTTP itself: status codes, saved copies of GET replies (caching), headers that prove who's asking. Part of REST's appeal is that it doesn't pretend to be a function call. A request is a message about a resource, and HTTP already says which methods are safe to repeat. A method is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT (replace) and DELETE are; POST isn't, as Production networking: load balancers, timeouts, retries and pools showed.

The details both programs must agree on, such as paths, fields and codes, are the contract. **OpenAPI** writes it down, in a file of JSON or YAML (a text format like JSON, with less punctuation). Version 3.2.0 came out in September 2025, and 3.2.1 in September 2026. Tools generate client code and documentation from the file, and CI, a program that builds and tests every change before it's accepted, can compare the new file with the last released one and stop a breaking change.

What counts as breaking follows from the order of deploys, the moments when a new version is installed and started. You deploy the server first, then the clients, which can take months for a phone app and forever for another company's program. So the new server must read old clients' requests: requests need backward compatibility, new code reading old data. And old clients must read the new server's replies: replies need forward compatibility, old code reading new data. These are the rules of Schemas that evolve, lesson 2 of this track. Adding an optional request field, or a reply field, is safe if clients ignore names they don't know. Removing, renaming or retyping a field breaks someone.

When a break can't be avoided, the API needs versions. The usual answer is `/v1/` and later `/v2/` in the path, which splits the server code in two, and old clients never move. Stripe, a company that takes card payments for many online shops, dates every breaking change instead. Each account is pinned to, meaning kept on, the version that was newest at its first request. A `Stripe-Version` header overrides the pin for one request. The server builds every reply in the newest shape. Then it runs the reply back through small change functions, one per breaking change, until it has the shape the caller expects. Since September 2024, only two named releases a year may break anything. The Try below plays the server's part.

Next, we'll meet gRPC, which starts from the contract and adds a deadline that travels with the call.

sections.h: gRPC: a contract file, binary messages and a deadline on every call

try.title: Follow one deadline through two services
steps: Open `DeadlineDemo.kt`. Three programs run inside one process. Checkout calls payments with a 300 ms deadline. Payments works for 120 ms, then calls the issuer (the bank that gave the customer the card) and sets no deadline of its own. The issuer needs 500 ms today.
Predict how much time the issuer sees left when its call arrives, and who gives up first.
Run it.

code.title: DeadlineDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
   0 ms  checkout calls payments with a 300 ms deadline
   1 ms  payments got pay-1, 299 ms left
 127 ms  issuer   got pay-1, 173 ms left
 311 ms  checkout gets DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
 312 ms  payments issuer call ended: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
 321 ms  issuer   sees the call cancelled, stops
```
Payments never set a deadline, yet the issuer saw 173 ms left: grpc-java passed on what remained of checkout's 300 ms. At about 310 ms, all three give up together. Without that, the issuer would have spent its full 500 ms on an answer nobody was waiting for, holding a thread the whole time. Timings vary by a few milliseconds from run to run.

sections.h: Spreading calls over copies: one connection, one backend
sections.body:
The payment service doesn't run as one program. It runs as three copies, called replicas, on three machines, so that a crash in one doesn't stop payments and the work is shared. Something must spread checkout's calls over them. That's a **load balancer**: one address that accepts connections and passes the work to one of the copies behind it, the backends.

Production networking drew the line between two kinds. An L4 balancer picks a backend when a TCP connection opens, then copies bytes both ways without reading them. (TCP carries a stream of bytes between two programs; L4 is its layer of the network, and L7 is HTTP's.) An L7 balancer reads each request and picks a backend for each one. A call centre's switchboard works like the L4 kind. It puts your call through to a free agent when the call starts. Keep the line open all day, ask three hundred questions, and the same agent answers all three hundred.

With HTTP/1.1, the older version, the difference hardly shows. A client's pool, a set of connections kept open for reuse, might hold 20 connections, spread over up to 20 backends. gRPC exposes it. A channel, gRPC's name for a client's link to a service, opens one HTTP/2 connection. Every call runs over it, in its own stream. Put an L4 balancer in front of three replicas, and the channel's one connection lands on one of them, and every call follows. In the Try below, 300 calls through an L4 proxy, a small program in the middle that does this job, arrive as 300, 0 and 0. Three channels give 100 each, but only because each opened its own connection.

There are three ways out. First, an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 and balances each stream. Envoy is a free one, and a service mesh puts one beside every program. Second, balancing in the client: it learns every replica's address and spreads its calls itself. grpc-java's `round_robin` policy, which takes the replicas in turn, does that. Third, as a quick patch, a server can cap how long a connection may live (`maxConnectionAge`), so clients reconnect every few minutes and get spread again.

The second fix raises a question every service has anyway: how does a client learn the addresses? That's **service discovery**. An address written into the client's code breaks when the server moves. DNS, the internet's directory that turns names into addresses, can return several. But every copy of a DNS answer is kept until it expires, so a dead address stays in use for a while (DNS: how a name becomes an address). A registry, a small database built for this job such as etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, tracks the live copies. Each copy registers its address and sends a heartbeat, an "I'm still here" message, every few seconds, and clients ask the registry. A mesh hides the whole question from your code, at the price of an extra proxy on every request's path.

Now each call reaches a healthy copy, and carries a deadline. But we're back at the fourth ending: the deadline fires, and nobody knows whether the card was charged. Next, we'll make it safe to ask again.

try.title: 300 calls, three replicas, three ways
steps: Open `BalancingDemo.kt`. It starts three copies of a gRPC service on 127.0.0.1, a small L4 proxy that picks a copy for each new TCP connection, and a name lookup that hands the client all three addresses at once, as DNS can.
Predict the three counts on each line before you run it.
Run it.

code.title: BalancingDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
one channel through the L4 proxy       replica-1=300  replica-2=0  replica-3=0
three channels through the L4 proxy    replica-1=100  replica-2=100  replica-3=100
one channel, client-side round_robin   replica-1=99  replica-2=102  replica-3=99
```
The proxy chose a copy once per connection, so one channel meant one copy. Three channels spread out only because they made three connections. With `round_robin`, the client keeps a connection to every copy and picks one per call. The counts are about 100, not exactly 100, because the first calls go out while the other connections are still opening.

sections.h: A retry is safe only with an idempotency key
sections.body:
Back to the fourth ending. Checkout got `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` for `pay-1`, and it has two choices. The Try below counts both over 1,000 payments, in which 30% of first replies are lost after the card was charged. If checkout gives up, 313 payments are reported as failed although every card was charged: customers paid for books nobody will send. If checkout retries, every payment succeeds, and 313 cards are charged twice.

On the phone, you'd say, "I'm calling about order 7F." The shop finds 7F in its order book and reads you the same receipt instead of packing a second parcel. In code, it's an **idempotency key**. The client makes one key per operation, here per payment, before the first attempt, and sends the same key with every attempt. Usually it's a UUID, a random 128-bit number, so two are practically never the same. The server claims the key before doing any work, stores the result under it, and answers every later request with that key from the store. The claim must be atomic: one step that no other request can get in the middle of. The Caching track's lesson Rate limiting and idempotency keys built that store in Redis, a database that keeps its data in memory.

Stripe's API has the best-known rules. The client makes the key, up to 255 characters. Once the work begins, Stripe saves the first request's status code and body, even a `500` error (a failure inside the server), and replays them for any retry with that key. Keys may be deleted once they're at least 24 hours old, so a retry after that is a new request. Reusing a key with different details is an error. A request that fails Stripe's checks, or arrives while another with the same key is still running, isn't saved, so it can be retried. Every POST accepts a key; GET and DELETE are idempotent already.

Three mistakes break keys in practice. A key made for each attempt, not for each payment, protects nothing; in the Try, that row is exactly as bad as no key. A key stored after the work, instead of claimed before it, lets two attempts both charge. That's the common case, because a retry after a timeout arrives while the slow first attempt is still running. And a key that stops at one service protects only that service. When the payment service calls the card's bank, it must send a key of its own, made from the client's (`k-7f/issuer`). Otherwise a crash between the bank's answer and the moment the payment service saves it charges the card twice anyway.

**A retry without a key is a second payment. Send the key.**

In gRPC, put the key in the request message, like field 3 of `ChargeRequest`. A header works too. But a field is part of the contract: it shows in the `.proto` file, it's logged with the request, and no proxy can drop it.

The phone picture breaks at the shop's end. A person might notice that two orders look alike. A server sees only bytes, so it can spot a repeat only by a key the client chose to send, and only for as long as it remembers that key. And a key makes only one call safe to repeat. An order that charges, reserves and ships makes three calls, and its program can crash between any two.

try.title: Count duplicate charges for four kinds of client
steps: Open `RetryDuplicatesDemo.kt`. One server and four kinds of client: no retries, retries without a key, retries with a new key on every attempt, and retries with one key per payment. A seeded random, which gives the same numbers on every run, picks the 30% of payments whose first reply is lost after the card was charged.
Predict the duplicates column for each row.
Run it.

code.title: RetryDuplicatesDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
client                      charges  duplicates  reported failed
no retry                       1000           0              313
retry no key                   1313         313                0
retry new key each time        1313         313                0
retry one key                  1000           0                0
```
313 payments were unlucky. Without retries, all 313 were charged and reported as failed: money taken, order not placed. Retrying without a key, or with a new key each time, fixes that and charges each of the 313 twice. Only one key per payment, sent on every attempt, gives 1,000 charges and no failures.

compare.title: The same charge as a REST call and as a gRPC call

a.label: REST over HTTP/1.1
a.title: request and response
a.src:
POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1
Host: api.payments.example
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 5f1c2a9e-8d43-4f2b-9b1e-7d0c3a6e2b41

{"payment_id":"pay-1","amount_cents":4000}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json

{"id":"ch_77","amount_cents":4000}

b.label: gRPC over HTTP/2
b.title: the frames, simplified
b.src:
HEADERS  :method POST   :path /payments.v1.Charges/Charge
         content-type application/grpc   grpc-timeout 300m
DATA     00 | 00 00 00 30 | 0a 05 70 61 79 2d 31 10 a0 1f 1a 24 ...
         flag | length 48 | field 1 "pay-1", field 2 4000, field 3 the key

HEADERS  :status 200   content-type application/grpc
DATA     00 | 00 00 00 0a | 0a 05 63 68 5f 37 37 10 a0 1f
HEADERS  grpc-status 0          (trailers: the real outcome)

compare.note: Both send the same charge with the same key. REST sends the field names as JSON text, puts the key in a header, and reports the outcome in the reply's first line, `201 Created`. gRPC sends 48 bytes of Protobuf, with field numbers instead of names and a 5-byte prefix in front of each message, and the key is a field of the message. Its HTTP status is 200 even when the call fails. The real outcome is `grpc-status` in the trailers, so a proxy that wants to count gRPC errors must read the trailers. The deadline is a header the server can act on (`300m` means 300 milliseconds). Plain HTTP has no standard way to tell the server how long the client will wait.

worked.title: Turn on gRPC's own retries, and see why the key still matters

steps.say: gRPC can retry for you. You describe the policy in the channel's service config, a map shaped like JSON: which method, how many attempts in all (the first one counts), how long to wait between them, and which status codes to retry. Retry only `UNAVAILABLE`, the code for "didn't get through".
steps.code:
val serviceConfig = mapOf(
    "methodConfig" to listOf(
        mapOf(
            "name" to listOf(mapOf("service" to "payments.v1.Charges", "method" to "Charge")),
            "retryPolicy" to mapOf(
                "maxAttempts" to 4.0, // the JSON numbers of a service config are doubles
                "initialBackoff" to "0.05s",
                "maxBackoff" to "1s",
                "backoffMultiplier" to 2.0,
                "retryableStatusCodes" to listOf("UNAVAILABLE"),
            ),
        ),
    ),
)

steps.say: Hand the config to the channel and switch retries on. (A service's owners can also publish a service config through the name lookup, and so set the policy for all their clients.)

Set one deadline per call. The lab's loop gives each attempt a deadline of its own. gRPC's policy works differently: it retries inside the call's original deadline, so here all the attempts together must finish within 2 seconds. That's also why `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` is usually left off the retry list.

`RetryPolicyDemo.kt` runs this against a server that charges the card and then loses every other reply. Every call succeeds and the program never sees an error, but 5 payments made 10 charges. The policy did exactly what it was told. Add an idempotency key to the request and a key store on the server, and each second attempt becomes a replay of the first.
steps.code:
$ ./gradlew :flow:demo -Pmain=sfz.enc.l04.demo.RetryPolicyDemoKt --console=plain -q
pay-0 -> ch_2
pay-1 -> ch_4
pay-2 -> ch_6
pay-3 -> ch_8
pay-4 -> ch_10
requests that arrived: 10, cards charged: 10 for 5 payments

lab.title: A gRPC client that retries safely, and the key store that makes it safe
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests once. All 11 fail: five in `IdempotencyStoreTest` and six in `ChargeClientTest`. The client tests start a real gRPC server inside the same program, with the in-process transport, so there's no Docker and no network port.

Read `ChargeRpc.kt` and `ChargeServer.kt`; both are finished. The first describes the `Charge` method and turns messages into Protobuf bytes by hand, with no code generator. The second holds the issuer, the `Faults` that lose or delay a reply after the charge, and the service itself.

In `IdempotencyStore.kt`, write `once`. Claim the key with `putIfAbsent`, and run the work only if your claim won. If the key was already there, compare fingerprints (a short summary of the request, such as `pay-1|4000`) and wait for the first result. Run `./gradlew :flow:test --tests 'sfz.enc.l04.IdempotencyStoreTest'` until its five tests pass.

In `ChargeClient.kt`, write `charge`. Make one key, then loop: give every attempt a fresh deadline, retry only the codes in `RETRYABLE`, wait a random time between attempts (full jitter, from Production networking), and stop after `maxAttempts`.
Run all 11. The last test charges 30 payments through a network that loses every third first reply. It expects exactly 10 duplicate charges without the key store, and none with it.
hints: `putIfAbsent` returns null to exactly one caller, and that caller does the work. Every other caller gets the winner's `Entry` and calls `entry.result.join()`, which waits if the work is still running.
Make the key before the loop. A key made inside it turns every attempt into a new payment, and the lost-reply test checks that the server saw only one key.
Catch `StatusRuntimeException` and look at `e.status.code`. If the code isn't in `RETRYABLE`, or this was the last attempt, throw `e` itself again, so the caller sees the real status.
If the slow-reply test takes a whole second, the deadline isn't set: pass `CallOptions.DEFAULT.withDeadlineAfter(...)` to `blockingUnaryCall`.

drill.title: Write the safe retry loop from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write `chargeWithRetries(channel, paymentId, cents)`: one idempotency key, a 200 ms deadline for each attempt, at most 4 attempts, retries only for `UNAVAILABLE` and `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and a random wait between attempts (full jitter) whose upper limit starts at 10 ms and doubles. Then compare with the answer. Did you make the key before the loop? Did you throw the last error again?

recap: A call to another program can end with no answer, and the caller can't tell a lost request from a lost reply. Waldo and his colleagues argued in 1994 that code must show this difference, not hide it.

REST names each thing with a URL and acts on it with HTTP's few methods, and OpenAPI writes the contract in a file that tools can check. Servers update first, so new servers must read old requests (backward compatibility) and old clients must read new replies (forward compatibility).

gRPC writes the contract in a `.proto` file and sends Protobuf messages over HTTP/2. It sets no deadline unless you do; a deadline travels as time remaining and follows the request into every call it causes.
A gRPC channel keeps one connection, so a balancer that picks a copy per connection sends all its calls to one copy. Balance each request in an L7 proxy, or in the client with `round_robin`.
Retry only with an idempotency key: made once per payment before the first attempt, claimed by the server before the work, and passed on to every program further down the chain.
The limit: a key makes one call safe to repeat. A job that makes several calls, such as an order that charges, reserves and ships, can still stop halfway when its program crashes between two of them.
closing:
We started with a Pay button that said "Something went wrong" and asked us not to press it twice. After a timeout, its program can't tell a lost request from a lost reply, and a second press carries nothing that lets the other side spot a repeat.

Pick an app you use that takes money, and ask what a second tap does if the answer to the first one gets lost. Stripe's API documentation shows one answer: an `Idempotency-Key` header on every POST.

Next, we'll follow an order that makes three calls, not one, and ask how it can survive a crash between any two of them.

quiz.q: Checkout calls the payment service with a 500 ms deadline. The payment service spends 200 ms on its own work, then calls the card's bank with grpc-java, without setting a deadline. How long can the bank's program work before its call is cancelled?
options: 500 ms, the original deadline
About 300 ms: the time remaining travels with the call
As long as it likes: nobody set a deadline on that call
200 ms
quiz.why: grpc-java hands the time left on the incoming call to any call made while handling it, and that time travels as time remaining. 500 minus 200 leaves about 300 ms. The third option is what happens to a call made outside any request, with no deadline of its own. That's why the first call in every chain needs a deadline.

quiz.q: A fraud-check service (a program that tests whether a payment looks stolen) runs as 6 copies behind a load balancer that picks a copy once per connection. Checkout runs as 2 copies, each with one long-lived gRPC channel to the fraud service. On a busy day, the fraud service grows to 12 copies. What happens to checkout's calls?
options: They spread evenly over the 12 copies within seconds
The balancer moves calls from busy copies to the new ones
Each call opens a new connection, so the new copies share the load at once
At most 2 fraud copies serve checkout, until those connections are closed and opened again
quiz.why: The balancer chooses once per connection, and each channel sends every call over its one HTTP/2 connection. So 2 channels reach at most 2 copies, and the new copies get checkout's calls only after a reconnect. The fixes: balance each request in an L7 proxy, let the client spread its calls with `round_robin`, or cap how long a connection may live.

quiz.q: You add `string currency = 4;` to `ChargeRequest` and deploy the new payment server before the clients. An old client sends a request without field 4. What does the new server see?
options: A parse error, because a field is missing
gRPC rejects the request with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`
`currency` is the empty string, Protobuf's default, so the server's code must decide that it means the old currency (EUR)
Field 3's value moves into field 4
quiz.why: A field missing from the bytes reads as its default value, here the empty string. That's what lets new code read old messages, the backward compatibility of Schemas that evolve. Nothing fails, so the server's code has to decide what an empty currency means. Neither Protobuf nor gRPC checks that every field is there.

quiz.q: A program sends `POST /v1/charges` to Stripe again, with the same `Idempotency-Key` and the same body, 30 hours after the first attempt, which worked. What can happen?
options: Stripe may have deleted the key by then, so the retry can create a second charge
Stripe always replays the first reply
Stripe rejects the request because the key is too old
Stripe answers 409 Conflict
quiz.why: Stripe keeps keys for at least 24 hours and may delete them after that. A deleted key makes the request new. Retries belong inside that window, which is why clients cap their total retry time. 409 Conflict is what a request gets while another one with the same key is still running.

quiz.q: A gRPC call to `Charge` fails with `INVALID_ARGUMENT: amount must be positive`. What should a well-built client do?
options: Retry with growing waits, since the server might recover
Retry once with a new idempotency key
Give up at once and report the error: the same request will fail the same way
Switch to another copy of the service and retry there
quiz.why: `INVALID_ARGUMENT` describes the request itself, not the network or the server's health, so every attempt gets the same answer. Retry `UNAVAILABLE` (it didn't get through) and, with a key, `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` (nobody knows). A new key wouldn't help either: it only makes the server forget that this is the same request.

flashcards.front: Which four differences between local and remote calls did Waldo and his colleagues name in 1994?
flashcards.back: Latency, memory access (a pointer means nothing in another program), partial failure and concurrency. Code should show them, not hide them.

flashcards.front: What does `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` tell you about a payment?
flashcards.back: Nothing about the outcome. The request or the reply may have been lost, or the server may still be working.

flashcards.front: What deadline does a gRPC call have if you set none?
flashcards.back: None at all. It can wait forever.

flashcards.front: Why does an L4 load balancer send all of a gRPC channel's calls to one copy?
flashcards.back: It picks a copy once per TCP connection, and a channel sends all its calls over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection.

flashcards.front: Where does a gRPC call's real outcome travel?
flashcards.back: In the trailers, as `grpc-status`. The HTTP status is 200 either way.

flashcards.front: How long does Stripe keep idempotency keys?
flashcards.back: At least 24 hours. After that it may delete them, and a retry counts as a new request.

flashcards.front: When does the client make an idempotency key?
flashcards.back: Once per operation, such as one payment, before the first attempt. Every retry sends the same key.

terms.plain: A program that keeps running on a computer and answers requests that other programs send it over the network.
Calling a function in another program, usually on another machine, through a stand-in function (a stub) that looks like a local call.
One part of a system fails while the rest goes on. For a call, it means no answer, and no way to tell what happened on the other side.
A style of API in which each thing has a URL and clients act on it with HTTP's methods, such as GET and POST.
A file format, in JSON or YAML, that describes an HTTP API: its paths, inputs, replies and status codes. Tools make client code, documentation and checks from it.
The moment after which a client stops waiting for a call. gRPC sends it as time remaining and passes it on to the calls it causes.
One address that accepts calls and passes each one to a copy of the service behind it. The L4 kind picks a copy per connection, the L7 kind per request.
A unique ID the client makes once per operation and sends with every attempt, so the server can answer a repeat with the first result.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "gRPC is a faster REST, nothing more, and retries are harmless inside one data centre, because the network there is reliable." Explain what's wrong with both halves.
explain_back.answer: gRPC is more than a faster REST. It's RPC with a Protobuf contract, one long-lived HTTP/2 connection per channel, a deadline that travels with each call, and its outcome in the trailers. The connection changes how calls get spread: a balancer that picks a copy per connection sends every call on a channel to one copy, so you need a balancer that reads each request, or a client that spreads its own calls. Browsers can't call it directly either. As for retries, even a reliable network loses replies when a program is stopped, a machine fails or a new version is rolled out, and a slow server looks exactly like a lost reply. After a timeout the client can't know whether the work was done. A retry without an idempotency key, made once per payment and claimed by the server before the work, can charge a card twice. Inside one data centre it only happens faster.

deeper.body:
Read Waldo and his colleagues' "A Note on Distributed Computing" in full; it's under 15 pages and has aged well. Its target was the 1990s hope of treating local and remote objects alike, which Java RMI, CORBA, Enterprise JavaBeans and SOAP all chased. Every argument in it applies to a generated gRPC stub that someone calls in a loop as if it were local. Around the same time, L. Peter Deutsch, also at Sun, listed the fallacies of distributed computing, beliefs that new distributed programs quietly assume: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, the layout of the network doesn't change, there is one administrator, and moving data costs nothing. James Gosling added an eighth around 1997: the network is the same everywhere.

Fielding's REST also asked for replies that carry links to the next possible actions, so a client could find its way through an API the way a person clicks through a website. Most APIs called REST skip that part.

Kubernetes, a popular program that runs copies of programs across many machines, makes the gRPC trap of the fourth section the default. Its usual way to reach a service is one address, balanced at L4, so copies added on a busy day get almost no gRPC calls until clients reconnect. A "headless" service makes its name lookup return every copy's address instead, so a client with `round_robin` can spread its own calls. Kubernetes also keeps the registry of live copies for you, so its programs rarely run etcd or Consul themselves.

Browsers can't make raw gRPC calls, because their HTTP interfaces hide HTTP/2's frames and trailers. gRPC-Web and Connect fill the gap. Connect, from a company called Buf, keeps the `.proto` contract; its servers answer gRPC, gRPC-Web and the Connect protocol, which also works over HTTP/1.1 and can be called with `curl` and JSON. Its Go, TypeScript and Swift libraries are stable; Kotlin is still beta.

Stripe names its versions by date and, since `2024-09-30.acacia`, gives each twice-yearly major release a name; the newest in November 2026 is `2026-10-28.endive`. In Stripe's v2 API, a retry drives a failed request to completion instead of replaying the stored error. The IETF, the body that writes internet standards, is working on a standard `Idempotency-Key` HTTP header; its draft reached revision 08 in October 2026 and is not yet an RFC.

gRPC has two more tools worth knowing. Hedging sends a second copy of a call if the first hasn't answered after a delay, and takes whichever answer comes first: good for cutting slow reads, dangerous on anything that changes data. And xDS lets gRPC clients take their balancing and routing settings from the same control program that drives Envoy, so a mesh can run without a proxy beside every program.

GraphQL takes a third path for APIs: one address, a typed schema, and clients that ask for exactly the fields they need. Its answer to versioning is never to break the schema: add fields, mark old ones as deprecated, and watch which clients still use them. The Data models track's lesson Triples, Datalog and GraphQL covers it as a query language.

For the book's view of services, service discovery and compatibility, see Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 5. Its point that servers update first, so requests need backward and replies forward compatibility, is the rule this lesson applied to REST, gRPC and Stripe's versions.
